warmup.q: Two cooks share one rail of slips. For one table, slip 3 says "starter" and slip 4 says "main course". Cook B takes slip 3 and cook A takes slip 4. Then cook B walks out before finishing, and the head chef clips slip 3 back at the front of the rail. Cook A finishes the main course, then takes the next slip. In which order do the dishes reach the table?
options: Starter, then main course: the rail is first come, first served, so the dishes are too
Main course, then starter: slip 3 reaches A only after A has finished slip 4
Only the main course: the starter's slip left with cook B
Starter, then main course: slip 3 went back to the front of the rail, ahead of slip 4
warmup.why: Slip 3 isn't lost, because it goes back on the rail when B leaves. It does go back to the front, which makes the last option tempting, but slip 4 had left the rail before B walked out, and A cooks it first. The rail kept its order; the kitchen's work didn't. Swap the slips for messages, the rail for a queue and the cooks for two copies of one program, and you have this lesson's biggest surprise. The third section steps through it, and the fourth measures how often it happens.

sections.h: Calling each program directly works until one of them is away
sections.html:
A small company runs the program that records card payments for many shops: which card paid, which shop, how much and when. At lunchtime it records about 1,200 payments a second. Three other programs need to hear about every one. The ledger keeps each account's balance. The fraud check looks for payments that seem stolen. And the receipts program emails each customer a receipt.

The program with the news is called the producer, and each program that needs it is a consumer. What travels between them is a message: a small piece of data such as auth acct-17 40.00 EUR. That one says account 17 has asked to pay 40.00 euros. (auth is short for authorization, the first step of a card payment, when the bank sets the money aside.)

Any way of moving messages from producers to consumers has to answer two questions. First, what happens when the producer sends faster than a consumer can keep up? There are three choices: drop messages, keep them in a buffer (a waiting area in memory or on disk), or slow the producer down. Making the sender slow down is called backpressure. Second, what is lost when a machine crashes or a consumer goes away?

The simplest design answers neither. The producer calls each consumer directly over the network, one message at a time. A common form is the webhook: each consumer gives the producer a web address, and the producer sends every message to it, the way a browser sends a form. Other direct designs drop whatever doesn't arrive, which is fine for a rough count of visitors and wrong for money.

All of these assume that both sides are up. Put numbers on it. The fraud check restarts for a two-minute update. At 1,200 payments a second, the producer must hold 144,000 messages, about 140 MB at 1 KB each, and send them later. Drop them, and the fraud check never sees two minutes of payments. Keep them in memory, and a restart of the producer loses them. Even a good day costs time: the receipts program takes 120 ms (thousandths of a second) to answer, and a producer that waits for it adds 120 ms to every payment.

The café solved this long ago with its rail. So put a program in the middle whose only job is to hold messages: a message broker. The slip is the message, the rail is a queue inside the broker, the cashier is the producer and the cooks are the consumers. The producer sends each message once, and waits only for the broker to say it has stored it. Consumers can be slow, restart or go away; their messages wait.

A broker is a kind of database, a program that stores data and answers questions about it, built for this one kind of traffic. It differs from an ordinary database in three ways. It deletes a message once a consumer has dealt with it, so it's no place to keep data for good. It expects short queues, and slows down when messages pile up and spill from memory to disk. And instead of answering questions, it sends each consumer the messages it subscribed to, as they arrive.

One payment still has to reach three consumers, though. Next, we'll open a broker and see how it makes the copies.

sections.h: Inside the broker: an exchange makes one copy for each queue
sections.html:
At the café, the kitchen and the bar may both need one slip, so someone copies it onto each rail. A broker has a part whose only job is that.

We'll use RabbitMQ, a free broker program that many companies run. Programs talk to it over the network using a protocol, a fixed set of rules for what each side sends and what it means. RabbitMQ grew up on one called AMQP 0-9-1, and that protocol also defines the broker's parts. There are three.

A queue holds messages in the order they arrived until consumers take them; it's the rail. An exchange is where producers send messages. It stores nothing. It only decides which queues get a copy, like the person who copies the slips. A binding connects an exchange to a queue, the way you'd tell that person "the bar wants every drinks order". Every message carries a label called a routing key, and each binding can carry a key of its own. The exchange's type says how the two must match:

Exchange type Puts a copy in
fanout every queue bound to it, whatever the key
direct each queue whose binding key equals the routing key
topic each queue whose binding pattern matches, such as payments.*.eur (* stands for any one word)
headers each queue whose conditions on the message's extra fields match

A default exchange with an empty name puts a message straight into the queue named by its routing key.

Two patterns come out of these parts. In fan-out, each consumer program gets its own queue, and all of them are bound to one exchange, so the ledger, the fraud check and the receipts program each receive every payment. In competing consumers, several copies of one program, called instances, read the same queue, and the broker gives each message to only one of them. Two ledger instances mean one crash doesn't stop the ledger, and twice the work gets done. Most systems use both patterns, as the figure shows: one queue per program, and a few instances on each queue.

With RabbitMQ's Java library, the figure takes a few calls. A channel is the program's line to the broker, opened over one network connection:

Java
channel.exchangeDeclare("payments", BuiltinExchangeType.FANOUT, true);          // durable
channel.queueDeclare("ledger", true, false, false, Map.of("x-queue-type", "quorum"));
channel.queueBind("ledger", "payments", "");                                    // fanout ignores the key
channel.confirmSelect();                                                        // turn on publisher confirms
channel.basicPublish("payments", "", MessageProperties.PERSISTENT_TEXT_PLAIN, body);
channel.waitForConfirmsOrDie(5_000);                                            // stored, or an exception
Kotlin
channel.exchangeDeclare("payments", BuiltinExchangeType.FANOUT, true)           // durable
channel.queueDeclare("ledger", true, false, false, mapOf("x-queue-type" to "quorum"))
channel.queueBind("ledger", "payments", "")                                     // fanout ignores the key
channel.confirmSelect()                                                         // turn on publisher confirms
channel.basicPublish("payments", "", MessageProperties.PERSISTENT_TEXT_PLAIN, body)
channel.waitForConfirmsOrDie(5_000)                                             // stored, or an exception

Line by line: declare the payments exchange as fanout; true makes it durable, so it survives a broker restart. Declare a queue ledger of type quorum: a quorum queue keeps every message on three machines by default, so losing one loses nothing. It's a Raft group, the kind Consensus with Raft built: the machines agree on every change before it counts. Bind the queue to the exchange with an empty key, which fanout ignores. Kotlin makes the same calls without semicolons, and writes Map.of as mapOf(... to ...).

The last lines matter most. confirmSelect asks the broker for a publisher confirm, a receipt for each message it has safely stored. waitForConfirmsOrDie waits up to 5 seconds for it, and throws an exception if the broker refused the message or never answered. For a quorum queue, RabbitMQ sends the receipt once most of the queue's copies, two of the three, have the message.

Java programs also meet Jakarta Messaging, long called JMS: a set of Java interfaces for talking to any broker, with queues for competing consumers and topics for fan-out.

The copies now reach their queues. Next, we'll see when a message may leave one, and what happens when a consumer crashes halfway.

try.title: One publish, three copies
steps: From the labs folder, start RabbitMQ 4.4 with docker compose -f env/rabbitmq.yml up -d --wait. Docker is a tool that runs programs in sealed boxes called containers, and this command starts RabbitMQ in one, in the background, with at most 512 MB of memory. It's ready in a few seconds. Then open a shell, a command prompt, inside it: docker compose -f env/rabbitmq.yml exec rabbitmq bash.

Run the block below. rabbitmqadmin is RabbitMQ's command-line tool. The block declares a fanout exchange payments and three quorum queues bound to it, publishes one payment, and takes one message from each queue.
Before you run it, predict: what will the second get on ledger return, and does it change what notify, the receipts program's queue, holds?
Keep the shell open for the next Try its.

sections.h: A message leaves only when it's acknowledged, and redelivery changes the order
sections.html:
A broker mustn't delete a message just because it sent it, since the consumer may crash halfway through. The kitchen has the same rule. A cook takes a slip, and it stays clipped above her station until the dish goes out. Only then is it thrown away.

So a consumer acknowledges each message, or acks it, once it has finished, and only then does the broker delete it. A message that was delivered and not yet acked is unacked: it stays in the queue, set aside for that consumer.

What if the consumer's connection closes before the ack, because the program crashed or the network dropped? RabbitMQ puts every unacked message back in the queue, at its old place when it can, and delivers it again with a flag, redeliver, set to true. That's redelivery. It gives you at-least-once delivery: no message is lost, and some are handled twice.

Why twice? Picture the ledger booking a payment (adding it to the balance) and crashing before its ack leaves. The broker can't tell that from a crash before the work started, so it sends the message again, and the consumer must spot the repeat. The worked example builds that.

You can switch acks off. With auto-ack, the broker counts a message as acknowledged the moment it sends it. RabbitMQ's own documentation calls that mode unsafe: a consumer that crashes loses every message it was holding. That's at-most-once delivery: nothing twice, and some never.

Most consumers should look like this:

Java
channel.basicQos(100);                                          // prefetch: the next section
channel.basicConsume("ledger", false, (consumerTag, d) -> {      // false: manual acks
    book(d.getBody());
    channel.basicAck(d.getEnvelope().getDeliveryTag(), false);  // ack only after the work is done
}, consumerTag -> {});
Kotlin
channel.basicQos(100)                                           // prefetch: the next section
channel.basicConsume("ledger", false, DeliverCallback { _, d ->  // false: manual acks
    book(d.body)
    channel.basicAck(d.envelope.deliveryTag, false)             // ack only after the work is done
}, CancelCallback { })

basicConsume subscribes to the ledger queue, and false turns auto-ack off. For each message d, the code in the middle books it, then acks it by its delivery tag, the number the broker gave this delivery. The ack comes last, after the work. Kotlin wraps the code in the library's DeliverCallback and reads d.body where Java calls d.getBody().

Redelivery has a cost few people expect: it changes the order. Each card payment takes two messages. When you tap your card, the bank first sets the money aside: that's the authorization, auth for short. Later the money really moves to the shop: that's the capture. The ledger must book the auth before its capture.

A queue is first in, first out (FIFO) at the moment it hands messages out, and only there. Step through it below. Two ledger instances share one queue, five messages for one account arrive, and one instance crashes. RabbitMQ puts m3 back at the head of the queue, but by then m4 has already left it. So the ledger books a capture before its auth.

AMQP and Jakarta Messaging both promise that a queue keeps its order, and this queue does. The order of the work doesn't, and the ledger only sees the order of the work. The café picture breaks here, too: a broker writes each message to disk on several machines before it says thanks, and it never knows whether a dish was cooked, only whether a cook said so.

A FIFO queue hands messages out in order. It can't make two consumers finish in order. Inside a broker, the fix is one consumer per queue, which RabbitMQ calls single active consumer, and that gives up competing consumers. The next two lessons show how a log keeps the order and still lets several consumers share the work.

How many messages should one consumer hold at once? Next, we'll see that the answer changes both speed and order.

The "next" message was m1 again: a returned message goes back to its old place, the head, ahead of m2. Its second delivery says redelivered: true, and the quorum queue counts the returns in a header, an extra field on the message, called x-delivery-count. x-acquired-count, new in RabbitMQ 4.3, counts every time a consumer took the message. A crashed consumer's unacked messages come back exactly like this; the only difference is that they all return at once.

sections.h: How much one consumer may hold: prefetch and backpressure
sections.html:
Picture a consumer that asks for one message, handles it, acks it, and only then asks for the next. After every message, it waits for a round trip: the time for a request to reach the broker and the answer to come back. With 2 ms of work and a 1 ms round trip, each message takes 3 ms. That's 333 a second instead of 500.

So brokers send messages ahead, the way a head chef hands a cook the next slips while she's still cooking. Prefetch caps how many unacked messages, or messages in flight, one consumer may hold at once. In AMQP the setting is basic.qos, which the Java library calls basicQos. RabbitMQ's documentation says values from 100 to 300 usually give the most messages handled per second, and quorum queues cap a consumer's prefetch at 2,000.

A bigger prefetch has a price. Every message a consumer holds is one more that comes back if it crashes, and one more that another instance can overtake. A slow consumer holding 1,000 messages also leaves the other instances idle, because the broker has promised those messages to it. And auto-ack has no prefetch limit at all: the broker sends as fast as the connection takes them. The Try it below measures all of this.

Prefetch is one kind of backpressure: the consumer says "no more until I ack". Every step between producer and consumer needs some:

  • TCP, the rules computers follow to send a stream of bytes over a network without losing any, has it built in. A receiver that stops reading makes the sender's writes wait (TCP performance, in the Computer networking track).
  • RabbitMQ pushes back on producers too. When a machine runs low on memory or disk, it stops reading from producers' connections. A queue with a length limit and overflow=reject-publish refuses new messages, and the producer sees a negative publisher confirm.
  • NATS JetStream, the storage part of another free messaging program, stops sending to a consumer holding 1,000 unacknowledged messages (its MaxAckPending default).
  • Amazon SQS, a queue you rent from Amazon's cloud, hides a received message for its visibility timeout (30 seconds by default, at most 12 hours), then shows it again if the consumer hasn't deleted it. Deleting is SQS's ack. A standard queue allows about 120,000 messages in flight, received but not yet deleted.

A log buffers in a different way. The next lesson shows that it keeps every message on disk until a time or size limit removes it, so a slow consumer only falls behind and slows nobody else down.

Redelivery saves a message from a crash. Next, we'll meet a message that crashes every consumer that takes it.

try.title: Count repeats, wrong orders and losses
steps: Run the demo from the labs folder (command below; no Docker needed). It pushes 1,000 payment messages for 10 accounts through a model of a queue kept in memory. The model counts time in ticks, steps of the model rather than real seconds. A consumer needs 1 to 3 ticks per message, and the crashing consumer dies every 25 ticks, just after finishing a message and before its ack.
Predict first. With one consumer that crashes, will any account's messages be booked out of order? With two consumers and no crash at all?

Look at the 2 consumers, prefetch 1 row. Why does it have duplicates but no inversions? (An inversion is a message booked after a later one of the same account. Hint: the 10 accounts were published in turn, so which messages are in flight at the same time?)
Run it again with -Pargs=10 for a crash every 10 ticks, and compare the auto-ack row.

code.title: RedeliveryDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.msg.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Set; import java.util.TreeMap; /** * 1,000 payment events for 10 accounts go through a broker queue, in memory, with no threads and no randomness. * Consumers take 1 to 3 ticks per message. A crashing consumer dies just after finishing a message and before its * ack, every N ticks (25 unless you pass another number), and comes back 5 ticks later. * For each setup the demo counts redeliveries, duplicates, per-account inversions and lost messages. */ public class RedeliveryDemo { record Message(String key, int seq) {} record Delivery(long tag, Message message, boolean redelivered) {} /** A queue with acks, prefetch and redelivery to the original position. */ static final class Queue { record Entry(long position, Message message, int returns) {} record InFlight(Entry entry, String consumer) {} final TreeMap<Long, Entry> waiting = new TreeMap<>(); final LinkedHashMap<Long, InFlight> inFlight = new LinkedHashMap<>(); final Map<String, Integer> prefetch = new HashMap<>(); final Set<String> autoAck = new HashSet<>(); long nextPosition = 0, nextTag = 1; void publish(Message m) { waiting.put(nextPosition, new Entry(nextPosition, m, 0)); nextPosition++; } void subscribe(String c, int max, boolean auto) { prefetch.put(c, max); if (auto) autoAck.add(c); } Delivery deliver(String c) { boolean auto = autoAck.contains(c); long held = inFlight.values().stream().filter(f -> f.consumer().equals(c)).count(); if (!auto && held >= prefetch.get(c)) return null; // at its prefetch var head = waiting.pollFirstEntry(); if (head == null) return null; long tag = nextTag++; if (!auto) inFlight.put(tag, new InFlight(head.getValue(), c)); return new Delivery(tag, head.getValue().message(), head.getValue().returns() > 0); } void ack(long tag) { inFlight.remove(tag); } void disconnect(String c) { List<Long> tags = inFlight.entrySet().stream().filter(e -> e.getValue().consumer().equals(c)).map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList(); for (long tag : tags) { Entry e = inFlight.remove(tag).entry(); waiting.put(e.position(), new Entry(e.position(), e.message(), e.returns() + 1)); // back to its old place } } } /** Consumers on one queue, one tick at a time. */ static final class Sim { final Queue q; final List<String> names; final int prefetch; final boolean auto; final List<Message> booked = new ArrayList<>(); final Map<String, ArrayDeque<Delivery>> held = new HashMap<>(); final Map<String, Delivery> working = new HashMap<>(); final Map<String, Integer> ticksLeft = new HashMap<>(); final Map<String, Integer> down = new HashMap<>(); int redelivered = 0; Sim(Queue q, List<String> names, int prefetch, boolean auto) { this.q = q; this.names = names; this.prefetch = prefetch; this.auto = auto; for (String c : names) { held.put(c, new ArrayDeque<>()); q.subscribe(c, prefetch, auto); } } static int cost(Message m) { return 1 + Math.floorMod(m.seq() * 7 + m.key().hashCode(), 3); } void tick() { for (String c : names) { Integer wait = down.get(c); if (wait != null) { if (wait > 1) down.put(c, wait - 1); else down.remove(c); continue; } ArrayDeque<Delivery> mine = held.get(c); while (mine.size() + (working.containsKey(c) ? 1 : 0) < prefetch) { Delivery d = q.deliver(c); if (d == null) break; if (d.redelivered()) redelivered++; mine.addLast(d); } if (!working.containsKey(c)) { Delivery next = mine.pollFirst(); if (next == null) continue; working.put(c, next); ticksLeft.put(c, cost(next.message())); } int left = ticksLeft.merge(c, -1, Integer::sum); if (left == 0) { Delivery done = working.remove(c); booked.add(done.message()); if (!auto) q.ack(done.tag()); } } } void crash(String c) { if (down.containsKey(c)) return; Delivery current = working.remove(c); if (current != null) booked.add(current.message()); // the work is done, the ack is lost held.get(c).clear(); q.disconnect(c); down.put(c, 5); // back in 5 ticks } void run(String crashing, int every) { int t = 0; while (!q.waiting.isEmpty() || !q.inFlight.isEmpty() || !working.isEmpty() || !down.isEmpty() || held.values().stream().anyMatch(h -> !h.isEmpty())) { t++; if (crashing != null && every > 0 && t % every == 0) crash(crashing); tick(); } } } static List<Message> payments() { List<Message> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) out.add(new Message("acct-" + i % 10, i / 10)); return out; } /** The row: booked, redelivered, duplicates, inversions, lost. */ static void row(String setup, List<Message> booked, int redelivered) { Set<Message> seen = new HashSet<>(); Map<String, Integer> highest = new HashMap<>(); int duplicates = 0, inversions = 0; for (Message m : booked) { if (!seen.add(m)) { duplicates++; continue; } Integer top = highest.get(m.key()); if (top != null && m.seq() < top) inversions++; else highest.put(m.key(), m.seq()); } System.out.printf("%-38s %6d %11d %10d %10d %5d%n", setup, booked.size(), redelivered, duplicates, inversions, 1000 - seen.size()); } static void oneQueue(String setup, List<String> consumers, int prefetch, boolean auto, int every) { Queue q = new Queue(); payments().forEach(q::publish); Sim sim = new Sim(q, consumers, prefetch, auto); sim.run(consumers.get(consumers.size() - 1), every); row(setup, sim.booked, sim.redelivered); } public static void main(String[] args) { int every = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 25; System.out.printf("1,000 payments, 10 accounts; a crash every %d ticks%n", every); System.out.printf("%-38s %6s %11s %10s %10s %5s%n", "setup", "booked", "redelivered", "duplicates", "inversions", "lost"); oneQueue("1 consumer, prefetch 10, no crash", List.of("A"), 10, false, 0); oneQueue("1 consumer, prefetch 10, crashes", List.of("A"), 10, false, every); oneQueue("2 consumers, prefetch 1, crashes", List.of("A", "B"), 1, false, every); oneQueue("2 consumers, prefetch 10, no crash", List.of("A", "B"), 10, false, 0); oneQueue("2 consumers, prefetch 10, crashes", List.of("A", "B"), 10, false, every); oneQueue("2 consumers, prefetch 100, crashes", List.of("A", "B"), 100, false, every); oneQueue("1 consumer, auto-ack, crashes", List.of("A"), 10, true, every); // one queue per half of the accounts, one consumer each: the way a log's partitions work Queue even = new Queue(), odd = new Queue(); for (Message m : payments()) (Integer.parseInt(m.key().substring(5)) % 2 == 0 ? even : odd).publish(m); Sim a = new Sim(even, List.of("A"), 10, false), b = new Sim(odd, List.of("B"), 10, false); a.run("A", every); b.run("B", every); List<Message> both = new ArrayList<>(a.booked); both.addAll(b.booked); row("2 queues by account, 1 consumer each", both, a.redelivered + b.redelivered); } }

redelivered: Boolean) /** A queue with acks, prefetch and redelivery to the original position. */ private class Queue { data class Entry(val position: Long, val message: Message, val returns: Int) data class InFlight(val entry: Entry, val consumer: String) val waiting = TreeMap<Long, Entry>() val inFlight = LinkedHashMap<Long, InFlight>() private val prefetch = HashMap<String, Int>() private val autoAck = HashSet<String>() private var nextPosition = 0L private var nextTag = 1L fun publish(m: Message) { waiting[nextPosition] = Entry(nextPosition, m, 0) nextPosition++ } fun subscribe(c: String, max: Int, auto: Boolean) { prefetch[c] = max if (auto) autoAck += c } fun deliver(c: String): Delivery? { val auto = c in autoAck if (!auto && inFlight.values.count { it.consumer == c } >= prefetch.getValue(c)) return null // at its prefetch val head = waiting.pollFirstEntry()?.value ?: return null val tag = nextTag++ if (!auto) inFlight[tag] = InFlight(head, c) return Delivery(tag, head.message, head.returns > 0) } fun ack(tag: Long) { inFlight.remove(tag) } fun disconnect(c: String) { for (tag in inFlight.filterValues { it.consumer == c }.keys.toList()) { val e = inFlight.remove(tag)!!.entry waiting[e.position] = e.copy(returns = e.returns + 1) // back to its old place } } } /** Consumers on one queue, one tick at a time. */ private class Sim(val q: Queue, val names: List<String>, val prefetch: Int, val auto: Boolean) { val booked = mutableListOf<Message>() private val held = names.associateWith { ArrayDeque<Delivery>() } private val working = HashMap<String, Delivery>() private val ticksLeft = HashMap<String, Int>() private val down = HashMap<String, Int>() var redelivered = 0 private set init { names.forEach { q.subscribe(it, prefetch, auto) } } fun tick() { for (c in names) { val wait = down[c] if (wait != null) { if (wait > 1) down[c] = wait - 1 else down.remove(c) continue } val mine = held.getValue(c) while (mine.size + (if (c in working) 1 else 0) < prefetch) { val d = q.deliver(c) ?: break if (d.redelivered) redelivered++ mine.addLast(d) } if (c !in working) { val next = mine.removeFirstOrNull() ?: continue working[c] = next ticksLeft[c] = cost(next.message) } val left = ticksLeft.getValue(c) - 1 ticksLeft[c] = left if (left == 0) { val done = working.remove(c)!! booked += done.message if (!auto) q.ack(done.tag) } } } fun crash(c: String) { if (c in down) return working.remove(c)?.let { booked += it.message } // the work is done, the ack is lost held.getValue(c).clear() q.disconnect(c) down[c] = 5 // back in 5 ticks } fun run(crashing: String?, every: Int) { var t = 0 while (q.waiting.isNotEmpty() || q.inFlight.isNotEmpty() || working.isNotEmpty() || down.isNotEmpty() || held.values.any { it.isNotEmpty() } ) { t++ if (crashing != null && every > 0 && t % every == 0) crash(crashing) tick() } } companion object { fun cost(m: Message) = 1 + Math.floorMod(m.seq * 7 + m.key.hashCode(), 3) } } private fun payments() = (0 until 1000).map { Message("acct-${it % 10}", it / 10) } /** The row: booked, redelivered, duplicates, inversions, lost. */ private fun row(setup: String, booked: List<Message>, redelivered: Int) { val seen = HashSet<Message>() val highest = HashMap<String, Int>() var duplicates = 0 var inversions = 0 for (m in booked) { if (!seen.add(m)) { duplicates++ continue } val top = highest[m.key] if (top != null && m.seq < top) inversions++ else highest[m.key] = m.seq } println("%-38s %6d %11d %10d %10d %5d".format(setup, booked.size, redelivered, duplicates, inversions, 1000 - seen.size)) } private fun oneQueue(setup: String, consumers: List<String>, prefetch: Int, auto: Boolean, every: Int) { val q = Queue() payments().forEach(q::publish) val sim = Sim(q, consumers, prefetch, auto) sim.run(consumers.last(), every) row(setup, sim.booked, sim.redelivered) } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val every = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 25 println("1,000 payments, 10 accounts; a crash every %d ticks".format(every)) println("%-38s %6s %11s %10s %10s %5s".format("setup", "booked", "redelivered", "duplicates", "inversions", "lost")) oneQueue("1 consumer, prefetch 10, no crash", listOf("A"), 10, false, 0) oneQueue("1 consumer, prefetch 10, crashes", listOf("A"), 10, false, every) oneQueue("2 consumers, prefetch 1, crashes", listOf("A", "B"), 1, false, every) oneQueue("2 consumers, prefetch 10, no crash", listOf("A", "B"), 10, false, 0) oneQueue("2 consumers, prefetch 10, crashes", listOf("A", "B"), 10, false, every) oneQueue("2 consumers, prefetch 100, crashes", listOf("A", "B"), 100, false, every) oneQueue("1 consumer, auto-ack, crashes", listOf("A"), 10, true, every) // one queue per half of the accounts, one consumer each: the way a log's partitions work val even = Queue() val odd = Queue() for (m in payments()) (if (m.key.removePrefix("acct-").toInt() % 2 == 0) even else odd).publish(m) val a = Sim(even, listOf("A"), 10, false).apply { run("A", every) } val b = Sim(odd, listOf("B"), 10, false).apply { run("B", every) } row("2 queues by account, 1 consumer each", a.booked + b.booked, a.redelivered + b.redelivered) }

The model has no randomness, so you get exactly these numbers, and the Java and Kotlin versions print the same table. One consumer never changes the order: returned messages go back to the head, and it takes them again in order. So its crashes only cost duplicates, one per crash, the message whose ack was lost. Crashes raise that to 131, and prefetch 100 to 357, with nearly 4,000 redeliveries. With prefetch 1, only two neighbouring messages are ever in flight, and neighbours belong to different accounts, so nothing is reordered. Auto-ack lost 459 of 1,000 payments. sections.h: A message that always fails, and what every queue forgets
sections.html:
Some messages can never succeed. Each night, the company pays every shop what it took that day, and the code calls each payout a settlement. One night a settlement message arrives with "amount": "forty", a word where a number should be. The consumer's code throws an exception, and the consumer crashes before its ack. The broker redelivers the message to the next instance, which crashes too. One bad message takes down every instance in turn, while the rest of the queue waits. This is a poison message.

The defence is a delivery limit: count how often a message came back, and stop after a set number of returns. Since RabbitMQ 4.0, quorum queues stop at 20 returns by default, and consumers see the count in a header, an extra field on the message, called x-delivery-count. Past the limit, the queue drops the message. Or, if the queue has a dead-letter exchange, it moves the message through that exchange to a dead-letter queue (DLQ), a queue for messages that failed. Every message there is a problem for a person: find the cause, fix it and send the message again, or decide it's safe to throw away.

A DLQ doesn't keep every message by default. Quorum queues move dead letters at most once: if the dead-letter queue can't take a message, it's gone, with no error anywhere. To move them at least once, you have to set dead-letter-strategy=at-least-once together with overflow=reject-publish on the source queue.

Every broker has its own words for the same ideas. Here are the ones you'll most likely meet, as of November 2026 (SNS is Amazon's service that copies each message to many subscribers):

Broker Competing consumers Fan-out Poison messages
RabbitMQ 4.4 several consumers on one queue an exchange bound to one queue per program delivery limit (20), then a dead-letter exchange
Apache Artemis (a Jakarta Messaging broker) a queue, or a shared topic subscription a topic a redelivery limit, then a dead-letter address
Amazon SQS and SNS consumers asking one SQS queue for messages an SNS topic sending to one SQS queue per program after maxReceiveCount receives, the DLQ
NATS JetStream several workers on one consumer one consumer per program on a stream MaxDeliver caps redeliveries

Now look at what every broker here keeps: a state for each message (waiting, unacked, given to whom, returned how often), and nothing once it's acked. That makes sharing work one message at a time easy, and it costs three things. A new program can't read last week's payments, because they're gone. Nobody can replay a day, reading it all again after fixing a bug. And competing consumers lose each account's order.

A queue forgets a message the moment it's acked. If anyone may need the past, keep it somewhere else.

The next lesson keeps every message in a log, a list that only grows at the end, and lets each reader keep one number: its place in the list. That's the idea behind Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages on disk and lets many programs read them. The demo's last row was a preview: one queue per half of the accounts, each with a single consumer, kept every account in order.

opening:
Picture the till at a busy café at lunch. The cashier takes your order, writes it on a slip and clips the slip to a rail above the kitchen hatch. She never waits for a cook, and if a cook steps out, the slips wait on the rail.

The company that records the café's card payments built its program the other way. After each payment, it calls three other programs and waits for each to answer. One day, one of them restarts for two minutes, and 144,000 payments have nowhere to go.

Calling the other program directly feels natural. It's how one function calls another, and it works on every quiet day. It fails on the day the other program is away.

Distributed SQL, the last lesson of Consistency and consensus, made many machines act as one database. Now we move data between programs. In this lesson, we'll put a rail between them, then crash a reader and feed it a message it can't read. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at a café rail that let the cashier keep serving while the kitchen caught up. A broker does the same for programs: the producer hands each message over once and moves on. The price is a set of rules. A message leaves only when it's acked, a crash brings it back, and two consumers can finish in the wrong order.

Think of a shop that emails you a receipt after you buy something. Have you ever had the same email twice? That's at-least-once delivery, seen from outside.

Next, we'll keep every message instead of deleting it, and ask what a reader must remember when nothing is ever thrown away.

compare.title: Count repeats and out-of-order bookings in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: static OrderCheck.Result check(List<Message> processed) { Set<Message> seen = new HashSet<>(); // equal by key and seq Map<String, Integer> highest = new HashMap<>(); // account -> highest seq booked so far int duplicates = 0, inversions = 0; for (Message m : processed) { if (!seen.add(m)) { duplicates++; continue; } // booked before: a redelivery after a lost ack Integer top = highest.get(m.getKey()); if (top != null && m.getSeq() < top) inversions++; else highest.put(m.getKey(), m.getSeq()); } return new OrderCheck.Result(processed.size(), duplicates, inversions); }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: fun check(processed: List<Message>): OrderCheck.Result { val seen = HashSet<Message>() // equal by key and seq val highest = HashMap<String, Int>() // account -> highest seq booked so far var duplicates = 0 var inversions = 0 for (m in processed) { if (!seen.add(m)) { duplicates++; continue } // booked before: a redelivery after a lost ack val top = highest[m.key] if (top != null && m.seq < top) inversions++ else highest[m.key] = m.seq } return OrderCheck.Result(processed.size, duplicates, inversions) }

compare.note: Both versions make the same two checks in one pass. A HashSet spots a repeat: seen.add(m) returns false when an equal message is already in the set. Message counts as equal when its key and seq match, because it's a Kotlin data class, which writes equals and hashCode for you. A map keeps the highest seq booked so far for each account, and anything lower is an inversion. Java reads the fields through getters (m.getKey()), Kotlin by name (m.key). In Kotlin, highest[m.key] may be null, and after the top != null check the compiler lets you compare it as a plain number. Java's Integer top needs the same check, or the comparison throws a NullPointerException. In Kotlin, if ... else gives a value, so the update fits on one line.

worked.title: Make a redelivered payment harmless: skip repeats, commit, then ack

steps.say: The ledger will see some payments twice: every crash between booking and ack causes one. So the producer gives each message a unique id when it creates it, called an idempotency key: two messages with the same id are the same payment. The consumer remembers which ids it has booked. Start by reading the id from the message. (Event is the consumer's own type for a message it has read, and channel is its line to the broker.)
steps.code: // 1. every event carries the id its producer gave it Event event = Event.parse(delivery.getBody()); long tag = delivery.getEnvelope().getDeliveryTag();

alt.html: // 1. every event carries the id its producer gave it val event = Event.parse(delivery.body) val tag = delivery.envelope.deliveryTag

steps.say: Record the id and book the payment in one database transaction, a group of changes the database makes all together or not at all. The table processed_events has the event id as its primary key, a column the database won't let two rows share. So a second insert of the same id changes nothing, and executeUpdate returns 0 rows. Book only when it returned 1. (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING is how PostgreSQL, a popular database program, says "skip a repeat"; other databases have their own way.)
steps.code: // 2. remember the id and book the payment, atomically try (java.sql.Connection db = pool.getConnection()) { db.setAutoCommit(false); try (PreparedStatement seen = db.prepareStatement( "INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING")) { seen.setString(1, event.id()); if (seen.executeUpdate() == 1) book(db, event); // first time: book it } // 0 rows: a repeat, book nothing db.commit(); }

alt.html: // 2. remember the id and book the payment, atomically pool.connection.use { db -> db.autoCommit = false db.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING").use { seen -> seen.setString(1, event.id) if (seen.executeUpdate() == 1) book(db, event) // first time: book it } // 0 rows: a repeat, book nothing db.commit() }

steps.say: Ack only after the commit, the moment the database has saved the transaction for good. If the program dies between commit and ack, the broker redelivers, the insert finds the id, nothing is booked twice, and this time the ack goes out. If the transaction itself fails, hand the message back with basicReject(tag, true). On a quorum queue that counts towards the delivery limit, so a payment that always fails ends up in the DLQ instead of going round for ever.
steps.code: // 3. ack after the commit, never before channel.basicAck(tag, false); // on an exception from step 2 instead: // channel.basicReject(tag, true); // requeue; counts towards the delivery limit

alt.html: // 3. ack after the commit, never before channel.basicAck(tag, false) // on an exception from step 2 instead: // channel.basicReject(tag, true) // requeue; counts towards the delivery limit

steps.say: Why not skip every message whose redeliver flag is set? Because the flag means "may have been seen", in both directions. A redelivered message may never have been booked, if the consumer died before starting, so skipping it loses a payment. And a repeat can arrive with the flag unset: a producer whose publisher confirm got lost sends the payment again, and the broker sees two separate messages. Only the id tells you for sure. Calling other services: REST, RPC and gRPC, in the Encoding, APIs and workflows track, made a retried request safe with the same idea.

In disconnect, copy the tags first (inFlight.filterValues { it.consumer == consumer }.keys.toList()). Removing entries from a map while you loop over it throws ConcurrentModificationException.

drill.title: Trace two consumers from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking back: one queue holds m1 to m5 for account acct-17. Consumers A and B have prefetch 2 and ack by hand. A takes m1 and m2; B takes m3 and m4. A books m1 and acks it. B books m3 and crashes before its ack leaves. A books m2 and acks it, then takes whatever is next, and from then on A handles everything. Write down the order in which the ledger books messages. Then count duplicates and inversions (messages booked after a later one of the same account) the way the lab's OrderCheck does.

answer.html:
booked: m1 (A), m3 (B), m2 (A), m3 (A, redelivered), m4 (A, redelivered), m5 (A)

B's crash returns m3 and m4 to the head of the queue, in their old order.
A's next two deliveries are m3 and m4, both with redeliver=true; then m5.

duplicates: 1   m3 was booked by B and again by A (B's ack was lost)
inversions: 1   m2 was booked after m3, before any redelivery: two consumers in parallel
                are enough to reorder. m4 and m5 are in order.

recap: Calling each consumer directly works only while both sides are up. A message broker in the middle stores each message until a consumer has dealt with it, so the producer never waits for a slow or missing consumer.

In RabbitMQ, producers send to an exchange, bindings decide which queues get a copy, and consumers read queues. One queue per program gives fan-out; several instances on one queue are competing consumers.

A broker deletes a message only when it's acked. A crashed consumer's unacked messages come back with redeliver=true, which is at-least-once delivery, so consumers must spot repeats. Auto-ack is at-most-once: a crash loses messages.
A queue is first in, first out when it hands messages out, not when consumers finish them. Competing consumers change an account's order, and redelivery and a large prefetch change it more.
Prefetch caps the unacked messages one consumer may hold (100 to 300 is typical). It's the consumer's backpressure, and the bigger it is, the more comes back after a crash.

The limit: a delivery limit (20 on quorum queues) and a dead-letter queue stop a poison message, but a broker forgets every message once it's acked. A new program can't read the past, and nobody can replay it. The next lesson's log keeps it all.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "We use a first-in, first-out queue with manual acks, so our four ledger instances book every account's payments exactly once and in order." Explain which parts of that are true and what you'd change.
explain.answer: Manual acks mean no payment is lost: the broker keeps a message until someone acks it, and gives it back if a consumer dies first. But that's at least once, not exactly once. An instance that books a payment and dies before its ack gets the payment sent to another instance, so the ledger needs an idempotency key on every message, and must skip ids it has already booked, in the same database transaction as the booking. The order claim is wrong too. The queue hands messages out in order, but four instances finish at their own pace, and a redelivered message arrives after later ones were already booked. For each account's order, I'd stop sharing one queue: send each account to one of several queues with one consumer each, or use single active consumer, or use the log of the next lesson, split by account.

deeper.html:
Direct messaging, by name. The designs with nothing in the middle from the first section have names you'll meet. Market data feeds in finance use UDP multicast: one network packet reaches many receivers at once, receivers spot gaps in the packets' sequence numbers, and they ask for the missing ones again, so the sender has to keep what it sent. ZeroMQ offers the same publish and subscribe pattern over TCP, with no server in the middle. StatsD sends counters over UDP and loses whatever doesn't arrive, which is why its numbers are at best close.

AMQP 1.0 and its flow control. AMQP 1.0, despite the name, is a different protocol from 0-9-1: it says how two programs pass messages, and leaves out the broker's parts. RabbitMQ 4.0 and later speak it too, and map its addresses, such as /queues/ledger, onto the same exchanges and queues. In 1.0, a receiver grants a sender link credit: a number of messages it may send. Credit is prefetch made explicit for each link, and a receiver can stop a sender by granting none. Each transfer then settles with an outcome. RabbitMQ maps accepted to an ack, released to a requeue and rejected to dead-lettering or a drop, and supports modified on quorum queues. RabbitMQ 4.0 made 1.0 a core protocol and reported more than double the peak throughput of 3.13 on some workloads.

What changed in RabbitMQ 4.x. 4.0 removed the older mirrored classic queues, so quorum queues and streams are the ways to replicate. 4.3 added 32 strict priority levels for quorum queues and consumer timeouts, which hand back messages a consumer has held too long. 4.4.0 (October 2026) added delayed messages. Apache ActiveMQ Artemis, the Jakarta Messaging broker, became a top-level Apache project of its own, Apache Artemis, in late 2025.

Two counters since RabbitMQ 4.3. Quorum queues now keep acquired-count, raised every time a message is returned for any reason, and delivery-count, raised only when a delivery failed. A client crash and basic.reject count as failures; according to the 4.3 release blog, a basic.nack and a consumer timeout raise only the acquired count. The delivery limit checks delivery-count, so a consumer that hands messages back without marking them failed can do so without limit.

Comparing brokers fairly. The 2011 Kafka paper (Kreps, Narkhede and Rao) measured about 400,000 messages a second from one producer sending batches of 50, against far less for ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ of the time. Its own authors note that the Kafka producer didn't wait for the broker's acknowledgement, while the other brokers kept track of every message's delivery state. A benchmark between systems means something only at equal guarantees.

Brokers keep moving. NATS Server 2.12 added atomic batch publish to JetStream: a batch is stored only if every message in it passes the stream's checks. RabbitMQ streams are an append-only log inside RabbitMQ, where reading deletes nothing, the same idea as the next lesson. And Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 12, frames this whole lesson around the two questions of the first section: what happens when producers outrun consumers, and what is lost in a crash.
